glosses: Dativ Plural des Substantivs Buzzer
auf den Buzzer schlagen, hauen, drücken

examples.text: Eigentlich hatten in den Blind Auditions nur die „Fanta Zwei“ für sie gebuzzert.
Bei Gewinnerin Charley Ann buzzerten nur Michi Beck und Smudo.

Lustig ist es auch, wenn nur Xavier Naidoo sich bei den vierten „Blind Auditions“ erweichen lässt, für Iveta Mukuchyans zwar hübsch aber etwas kraftlos gesungenes „Euphoria“ zu buzzern und ihr dann sagt: „Es war an vielen Stellen so eigen, dass ich dachte, man sollte dir eine Chance geben.“
Auch bei Germany's Next Topmodel buzzern die Juroren nun um ihre Favoritinnen.
Vier Juroren sitzen mit dem Rücken zur Bühne und wenn das gefällt, was sich hinter ihnen abspielt, buzzern sie drauf los.

translations.source_sense_description: intransitiv, meist im mündlichen Gebrauch: auf den Buzzer schlagen, hauen, drücken

glosses: A continuous humming noise, as of bees; a confused murmur, as of general conversation in low tones.

examples.text: In the steady buzz of flies the homeward-bound agent was lying flushed and insensible[.]

This probably explains the interest in UVB-76, or “The Buzzer,” a mysterious shortwave radio station that has been operating since 1982 and whose output consists of a monotonous buzz repeated 24 hours a day, occasionally interrupted by a Russian voice.

glosses: A whisper.
The audible friction of voiced consonants.
A rush or feeling of energy or excitement; a feeling of slight intoxication.

examples.text: Still feeling the buzz from the coffee, he pushed through the last of the homework.

glosses: A telephone call or e-mail.

examples.text: Now, don't waste time, give us a buzz -- quick! 825-4703 or 265-7881.

glosses: Major topic of conversation; widespread rumor; information spread behind the scenes.

examples.text: Mr. Hall? The buzz on Christian is that his parents have joint custody, so he'll be spending one semester in Chicago and one semester here.
I wasn't performing with Pimp and Smoove that much no more, but I had a solo deal with Ruthless Rap and a brand new mixtape that was creating a big buzz.
In Detroit, the buzz is that he's too nice a guy, unwilling to impose draconian job cuts at the risk of angering the UAW.

Allen Gregory DeLongpre: Who's he?
Patrick: He's only the most popular kid in school.
Allen Gregory: Ah, the two heavyweights finally meet. Sure you're tired of all the buzz. Allen Gregory DeLongpre.

glosses: Synonym of fizz-buzz (“counting game”).
To make a low, continuous, humming or sibilant sound, like that made by bees with their wings.

examples.text: Ah! the singing, fatal arrow, / Like a wasp it buzzed, and stung him [a roebuck]!

So that now the universe has escaped from the pin which was pushed through it, like an impaled fly vainly buzzing: now that the multiple universe flies its own complicated course quite free, and hasn't got any hub, we can hope also to escape.

glosses: To make a low, continuous, humming or sibilant sound, like that made by bees with their wings.
To utter a murmuring sound; to speak with a low, humming voice.

examples.text: However these disturbers of our peace / Buzz in the people's ears.

glosses: To make a low, continuous, humming or sibilant sound, like that made by bees with their wings.
Of a group of people, to talk about some interesting topic excitedly.

examples.text: But I tell you this has set all London buzzing. The old man is where he likes to be, with a pin-point limelight right on his hairy old head.

glosses: To make a low, continuous, humming or sibilant sound, like that made by bees with their wings.
To fly while making such a sound.

examples.text: The flies, lethargic with the autumn, were beginning to buzz into the room.
A fly was buzzing past me.

glosses: To show a high level of activity and haste, energization or excitement, to be busy as a bee in one’s actions but perhaps mentally charged.
To whisper; to communicate, as tales, in an undertone; to spread, as a report, by whispers or secretly.

examples.text: I will buzz abroad such prophecies / That Edward shall be fearful of his life.

glosses: To talk to incessantly or confidentially in a low humming voice.
To fly at high speed and at a very low altitude over a specified area, as to make a surprise pass.

examples.text: […] an asteroid a mere 15-20 metres across exploded with the force of a medium-sized atom bomb over Chelyabinsk, in Russia, and another, much larger one buzzed Earth a few hours later.

glosses: To cut (the hair) in a close-cropped military style, or buzzcut.

examples.text: Deacon said, “You used to beg me to let you buzz your hair when you were little.” “And then I grew up and realized how awful you looked when you buzzed yours.”

glosses: To throw swiftly.

examples.text: I have mentioned her deft hand with a stone — well, as soon as our backs were turned she buzzed a stone to clip Joe's ear.

glosses: To drink to the bottom.

examples.text: He buzzed the bottle with such a hearty good will as settled the fate of another, which Soapey rang for as a matter of course. There was but the rejected one, which however Spigot put into a different decanter and brought in […]

glosses: To communicate with (a person) by means of a buzzer.

examples.text: Then one day my secretary buzzed me and said Frank Sinatra was on the phone. When I picked up the phone it was the Chief who played dumb and would not admit that he said he was Frank Sinatra.

translations.source_sense_description: intransitiv, meist im mündlichen Gebrauch: auf den Buzzer schlagen, hauen, drücken

glosses: Émettre un bourdonnement en parlant principalement des battements d’ailes des insectes, des petits oiseaux.

examples.text: Et soudain, au chocs des pots, aux grincements de la guitare, au rire des servantes, au brouhaha de la foule, succéda un silence à travers lequel eût bourdonné le vol d’une mouche.
De cette façon, ils ne perdirent pas de vue les abeilles […] ; elles entrèrent après avoir bourdonné un moment, dans un trou situé à plus de quatre-vingts pieds du sol.
Les colibris bourdonnent autour de cet arbrisseau.

glosses: Fait qu’un objet, qu’une machine, qu’une surface émette des vibrations plus ou moins sonores.

examples.text: Tu m’as dit avoir éteint le moteur pourtant je l’entends bourdonner.
Le sol bourdonne c’est à cause des travaux à proximité.

La lumière a ses chants.
C’est pour leur cri que j’aime les feux.
Alors que les mèches des chandelles durant des siècles grésillèrent, le fil électrique bourdonne.
Partout on retrouve ce bourdon propre à la lumière électrique dans le monde.
C’est la « tonalité » du monde.

glosses: Quand un grand nombre de personnes émettent un murmure sourd et confus en discutant entre elles.

examples.text: Lorsqu’elle passait, ils bourdonnaient de médisance.

Je perdis la connaissance et le sentiment : j’entendais seulement bourdonner autour de moi des voix confuses et lointaines ; soit qu’elles parlassent, soit que les oreilles me tintassent, je ne distinguais rien que ce tintement qui durait.
Quand il eut cessé de parler, on entendit bourdonner toute l’assemblée.

glosses: Ressentir un bruit sourd et lancinant dans sa tête.

examples.text: Les oreilles me bourdonnent ou alors j’ai les oreilles qui bourdonnent.

glosses: S’agiter, bouillonner en parlant d’un lieu ou de personnes.

examples.text:
— Eh bien ! Ça bourdonne dans les locaux de la direction. Qu’est-ce qui se passe ?
— Visite surprise de l’inspection du travail.

glosses: Fredonner une chanson à mi-voix entre ses dents.

examples.text: Il bourdonne toujours quelques vieux airs.

glosses: Importuner par des paroles, des lamentations, des discours.

examples.text: Que venez-vous nous bourdonner sans cesse ?
Il nous bourdonne ses soucis mais peu l’écoutent.

glosses: Faire résonner une cloche sans la sonner en branle.

examples.text: Les cloches bourdonnent sourdement dans la tour pour le moine qui vient d’expirer.

glosses: Émettre un bourdon.

examples.text: Deux cordes de la vielle bourdonnent un fond sonore car elles ne sont pas affectées par les touches contrairement aux autres qui servent à jouer la mélodie.
